Workbook 04 • Truth Lab

Can You Trust It?

Fake news, misinformation, context and deepfakes. Every click leaves a trail. Follow the ripple, weigh the impact and choose what happens next.

Year 8 ICT & Computer Science
ACTIVITY EDITION 4 · Matching, ranking and real-world cases
Truth Tracker badgeComplete the core route to unlock
YOUR SECTOR • Truth Lab

Meet Truth Lab

Know the themes. Meet the people. Explore several everyday situations.

Fake news, misinformation, context and deepfakes

Investigate a crowded feed, an old announcement and a cropped clip. Decide what you can confirm before a claim reaches more people.

Misinformation

False or misleading information. “Fake news” is a broad label; identify the actual problem, such as a wrong date or missing context.

Disinformation

False or misleading information spread deliberately to deceive. A wrong post alone does not prove the sharer’s intention.

Evidence and AI

Check the original source, date and context. AI can alter faces and voices; looking convincing or odd does not settle authenticity.

Ellis

Enjoys drama and gaming. A clip of a character he plays can misrepresent his own views.

Seren

Asks where a claim came from, even when everyone else is already forwarding it.

By the end, you will be able to:
  • Separate claims from evidence
  • Judge source usefulness
  • Correct without spreading harm

Use the fictional details given. You never need to share a personal incident.

EXPLORE • Truth Lab

Claim, evidence or opinion?

Apply the key ideas from your sector briefing.

→
Sort the feed items.

Evidence literacy: A claim can be checked, an opinion expresses a judgement, and evidence can help test a specific claim.

Claim, opinion or relevant evidence?

Choose a match for each card, then check the set. You can revise your matches after feedback.

Do not guess the motive

A person may share a wrong post by mistake. Calling it deliberate disinformation needs evidence of intention.

PRACTISE • Truth Lab

Which source first?

Compare different events and explain what matters.

→
Rank the checks for this claim.

Evaluate sources: Judge relevance, date and independence, not just confidence or popularity.

NEW CLAIM

“School is closed tomorrow”

A screenshot spreads through a family chat. The message has no date, but a cousin says “everyone’s seen it”.

Which route would you check first?

Use ↑ and ↓ to order the cards. First = highest priority. Several orders may be defensible; your explanation matters.

  1. Three friends’ reposts

    All three use exactly the same screenshot.

  2. An official notice from last winter

    It is genuine, but it describes a different date.

  3. The current official school channel

    Check for a dated announcement about tomorrow; ask school if it is still unclear.

  4. Comments beneath the screenshot

    Strangers confidently say it is true, without linking to a source.

Why is your first route stronger than one lower down? Identify a specific difference.

THINK DEEPER • Truth Lab

Restore the context

Use clues, consider perspectives and test your judgement.

→
Read the short clip, then restore its context.

Revise an inference: Changing your view when evidence changes is a strength.

FICTIONAL SCREEN
Seven-second clip · transcript
Shared caption

“Ellis finally admits what he thinks of the club.”

Ellis in the clip

“This club is a joke.”

What impression does the caption encourage? Treat it as an impression, not an established fact.

Reveal the longer transcript and source

Fictional evidence: the drama teacher supplies the full rehearsal recording through the usual school channel. Ellis is playing a character. The line before his is: “Read the villain’s next line, Ellis.”

How does the new context change the claim about Ellis’s own views?

How could the misleading caption affect Ellis at rehearsal or in a friendship?

TAKE ACTION • Truth Lab

Correct without amplifying

Turn your understanding into a practical response.

→
Draft a family-chat correction.

Correct constructively: Be specific and respectful, and avoid giving the misleading post another audience.

FICTIONAL CHAT
Family chat
Uncle

The town library is closing for good. Such a shame. [Screenshot]

Your check

The screenshot is from two years ago. The current library notice says it closes for one afternoon for maintenance, then reopens.

Practice draft · Your reply to the family

Give the current information and the checking route.

Suggest what to do with the old message. Do not mock your uncle or repost the screenshot.

Your sentences will appear together here.
Nothing is sent. Check how your message would land.
STRETCH • Truth Lab

AI is not the only explanation

Take the optional Truth Tracker challenge route.

Optional challenge · explain the tension, then defend a practical response.

UNCONFIRMED MEDIA

“The mouth looks odd. It must be AI.”

A friend shares a low-quality video apparently showing a local coach insulting a player. The audio is out of sync. The original recording has not been found.

Give TWO possible explanations for the odd appearance. Do not assume either is true.

What evidence would help distinguish the explanations? What should you do with the clip while checking?

CLOSE • Truth Lab

Your verification habit

Lock in the key idea and prepare to save.

Your friend says “Loads of people shared it, so it must be true”. Give a better checking rule.

Before you collect your badge

Completion checks show that you have responded. Your teacher reviews the quality of your reasoning. Save your completed HTML file to your ICT/CS folder, then upload that file to the assignment.

If something like this is happening to you, speak privately to a trusted adult or use your school’s reporting route.

Ripple City field guide

Key terms

MisinformationFalse or misleading information. “Fake news” is a broad label; identify the actual problem, such as a wrong date or missing context.
DisinformationFalse or misleading information spread deliberately to deceive. A wrong post alone does not prove the sharer’s intention.
Evidence and AICheck the original source, date and context. AI can alter faces and voices; looking convincing or odd does not settle authenticity.
DeepfakeSynthetic or altered media that convincingly imitates a real person.
CorroborateCheck whether independent reliable sources support a claim.
ContextThe surrounding facts needed to interpret something fairly.
SourceWhere information or media originally came from.
